title: Too Much Transparency Can Be a Bad Thing
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece pushes back on the assumption that more transparency is always better leadership practice. The author argues that sharing information too early in a decision process — before a conclusion is reached — can do more harm than good, because people act on expectations rather than facts. Using the example of a company exploring a headquarters relocation, the piece walks through how premature openness can trigger anxiety, rumor, and even the departure of valued employees before a decision is ever finalized. The core distinction drawn is between transparency as a value and timing as a skill: leaders must weigh not just whether to share information but when. The piece lands on a middle position — withholding information until people need it disrespects them, but assuming people won't act on early information is naive.
points: Timing, not just openness, determines whether transparency helps or hurts a team's stability.
Sharing a decision-in-progress can cause people to act as though the decision is already final, even when it may never happen.
The relocation example illustrates how premature disclosure can cost an organization valued employees who leave in anticipation of a change that never materializes.
Leaders are challenged to balance two failure modes: excluding people from the process versus giving them information they'll act on prematurely.
quotes: Good leaders today are much more transparent and open than leaders of the past.

To engage team members and include them in decisions that affect them, leaders often share information about the early stages of a decision and how it is shaping up, even before a conclusion is reached.
Because people act on expectations, complete openness and transparency is a fool’s errand, ripe with dysfunction.
Too little information and leaders are accused (accurately) of being parental and excluding others from the process.
Too much information and team members will act as if a decision is already made, even though the idea may fizzle and be discarded.
Unfortunately, some valuable employees will leave in anticipation of a decision that never happens.
The idea that leaders can and should be fully transparent at all times is nonsense.
To hide or protect information until team members NEED to know is to treat people disrespectfully and like cogs in a wheel.
This is the push and pull of artful leadership and it is never easy.
